What our research said: Kenya imported about 50,592 tonnes of petroleum bitumen worth about USD 27.5 million in 2023.
What the sources say: Confirmed: 50,591,822 kg worth USD 27,511,093 in 2023, an average of about USD 544 per tonne.

What our research said: Kenya imported about 39,850 tonnes of petroleum bitumen worth about USD 20.1 million in 2024.
What the sources say: Confirmed: 39,850,049 kg worth USD 20,145,616 in 2024, an average of about USD 506 per tonne.

What our research said: Most of Kenya's bitumen comes from Gulf-region suppliers, mainly Iran and the UAE.
What the sources say: 2023: Iran 32.6%, Turkey 26.2%, UAE 21.2%, Kuwait 12.0%, Oman 2.2%, Bahrain 2.1%, Iraq 2.0%, India 1.0% (by weight). 2024: UAE 36.6%, Iran 31.5%, Kuwait 12.2%, Oman 9.1%, China 4.3%, Turkey 3.8%, Bahrain 1.3%, India 1.3%. Gulf-region suppliers provided about 72% of the weight in 2023 and about 91% in 2024.
Note: Computed from the partner-level weights returned by the UN Comtrade preview API. Country codes follow UN M49 (364 Iran, 784 UAE, 414 Kuwait, 792 Turkiye, 512 Oman, 48 Bahrain, 368 Iraq, 699 India, 156 China).

What our research said: Kenya's bitumen import bill is about USD 20-28 million a year (about KES 2.6-3.9 billion).
What the sources say: The recorded import bill was USD 27.5 million in 2023 and USD 20.1 million in 2024, roughly KES 2.6-3.9 billion at the exchange rates of those years. Wider indirect costs (delays, risk premiums) are our own estimate and are not sourced.

What our research said: The Kenyan shilling has traded at about KES 129 per US dollar in 2026.
What the sources say: The shilling traded at about KES 128.6-130.3 per USD during 2026 (129.30 on 31 July 2026) and has been broadly stable.

What our research said: Kenya has about 239,000 km of public roads, of which about 24,000 km are paved.
What the sources say: 239,000 km in June 2024 (165,000 km classified, 74,000 km unclassified). Roads under bitumen: 23,000 km in 2023 and 24,000 km in 2024.

What our research said: KES 171.9 billion in FY2024/25, with 69.5 billion for repairs and maintenance (Phase 2)
What the sources say: Confirmed: total roads budget KES 171.9 billion for 2024/25; maintenance and repair rose from KES 66.5 to 69.5 billion.

What our research said: About KES 400 billion was needed to clear Kenya's road maintenance backlog (reported 2020).
What the sources say: About KES 400 billion was required for backlog maintenance, with a further KES 100 billion a year and a funding shortfall of KES 300 billion a year (Kenya Roads Board figures reported in February 2020). Because of the date, read it as indicative.

What our research said: In 2023, 30% of Kenya's road network was in poor condition and 46% in fair condition.
What the sources say: A 2023 inventory and condition survey found 30% of the network in poor condition and 46% in fair condition.
Note: Figure seen in search results; the article page itself could not be opened for a second read.

What our research said: Overloaded trucks shorten the life of roads.
What the sources say: An engineer told The Standard that a road designed for 15 years lasts about 5 under gross overloading (2015), and a University of Pretoria study estimates Kenya loses around USD 43 million a year to overload damage.
Note: The USD 43 million figure appeared in search results for the Pretoria study; we have not read the full study.

What our research said: Kenya's maximum pavement design temperature is about 64 C.
What the sources say: A Superpave temperature-zoning study for the Great Lakes region reports a maximum pavement design temperature of 64 C for Kenya.

What our research said: Kenya generates 0.5-1.3 million tonnes of plastic waste a year, of which about 8% is recycled.
What the sources say: Estimates are higher: 0.5-1.3 million tonnes a year, of which about 8% is recycled (Kenya Plastics Pact). UNEP's SMEP programme reports more than 966,000 tonnes. Other sources give recycling at 2-8% (NEMA), 7% (USAID) or 15% (an NEMA official, 2020).

What our research said: Kenya generates more than 3 million waste tyres a year.
What the sources say: More than 3 million waste tyres a year, growing about 10% a year. In 2024 about 3.2 million were generated and roughly 0.4 million (11%) recycled.

What our research said: Up to about 280,000 tonnes of used cooking oil could arise in Kenya each year.
What the sources say: Kenya consumes about 700,000 tonnes of vegetable oil and fat a year and about 40% ends up as waste, which implies up to about 280,000 tonnes. Only a fraction is collected. Eni has exported used cooking oil collected in Nairobi for biorefining, and GilOil produces biodiesel from it.
Note: Only a fraction is collected. Competing demand (export, biodiesel) means not all oil is available for roads.

What our research said: Kenya produces about 2.4 million tonnes of bagasse a year; about 1 million tonnes is dumped or burned.
What the sources say: About 2.4 million tonnes of bagasse a year is produced. Much of it is burned to power the mills (for example the 35 MW Mumias and 40 MW West Kenya co-generation plants). Roughly one million tonnes a year is dumped or burned, about 40%.
Note: Bagasse already has a competing use (power), which matters for a clean-energy audience.

What our research said: Kenya is a net importer of alginate, and red seaweed is farmed in Kwale.
What the sources say: Kenya is a net importer of agar and alginate, and Eucheuma and Kappaphycus are farmed in Kwale. Supply of brown seaweed (Sargassum, the usual alginate source) in Kenya is not yet established.
Note: Our plan is to import alginate first, which avoids depending on local brown seaweed.

Topic: Calcium alginate capsules survive asphalt production
What our research said: Calcium-alginate capsules containing a rejuvenator survive asphalt production.
What the sources say: Confirmed in published TU Delft work: calcium alginate capsules holding a rejuvenator survived asphalt production and compaction, and showed a healing effect on asphalt mastic. Capsules in porous asphalt kept a perfect round shape under X-ray tomography.

Topic: How much do capsules heal cracks?
What our research said: Calcium-alginate capsules can improve the healing of cracks in asphalt; results depend on temperature and capsule design.
What the sources say: Published results vary widely. One porous-asphalt study at 23 C found capsules raised healing by about 6 percentage points (maximum 19%); other studies report up to about 80% healing, and a capsule mix recovering 52.9% of strength at 20 C against 14.0% without capsules. Heating above 40 C is reported to have a significant effect on healing.
Note: The animation and simulator use an illustrative model. Its numbers are our own estimates, not published values.

Topic: Do capsules break only at cracks?
What our research said: Capsules are designed to stay shut in everyday traffic and to open at crack tips.
What the sources say: Partly confirmed: capsule rupture under load is documented. One study reported more than 80% capsule rupture after 350 cycles at 0.6 MPa, which means capsules can also break under repeated heavy load, not only at cracks. Our statement that they ignore everyday traffic is a design intent, not a proven result.

What our research said: Waste plastic is already used in roads in several countries.
What the sources say: India has built about 2,900 km of national highways and about 40,000 km of rural roads using waste plastic (as of 2024). Ghana is cited among countries using plastic in roads. South Africa was only 'embarking' on plastic roads in 2019, so it is not a major example.

Topic: Plastic improves rutting and fatigue resistance
What our research said: Recycled plastic at about 6% of the binder improves rutting and fatigue resistance.
What the sources say: Supported: reviews report that recycled PE and PP improve rutting and fatigue resistance, and that the best results are usually at 3-8% plastic in the wet method. Our 6% sits in that range. Exact percentage gains in Phase 4 are our own predictions.

Topic: Polyethylene separates from bitumen unless a compatibiliser is used
What our research said: A compatibiliser additive stops polyethylene separating from bitumen.
What the sources say: Supported: PE-modified bitumen shows severe phase separation because of poor compatibility, and maleic-anhydride grafting is a documented way to improve compatibility.

What our research said: Whether plastic-modified roads release microplastics.
What the sources say: Not yet settled. Studies estimate microplastic release from plastic-modified pavement at about three orders of magnitude below tyre-wear particles, but it is still uncertain whether particles are released under normal wear. This is an open research question.

Topic: Waste cooking oil as a bitumen rejuvenator
What our research said: Waste cooking oil can rejuvenate aged bitumen.
What the sources say: Supported by laboratory studies: waste cooking oil softens and rejuvenates aged bitumen and improves low-temperature behaviour and fatigue life, at some cost to rutting resistance. Commercial bio-based rejuvenators exist (for example Cargill Anova and Sylvaroad). A 2026 study found 5% dosages kept good fatigue performance after ageing, while 10-15% caused excessive softening.

What our research said: Warm Mix Asphalt cuts plant fuel use by about 20%.
What the sources say: Measured savings are around 20-22%: an average of 22.1% across six plants (West et al.) and about 20% in a multi-state study.
